justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from a presumed current level near 87–88. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the current price with minimal drift, expecting typical overnight and intraday mean-reversion dynamics to keep the asset near its recent trading range. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for slightly more drift upward, reflecting a mild positive momentum assumption that often holds over short horizons in trending markets, while also acknowledging that a week provides enough time for new information to shift sentiment. At the one-month horizon, I extended the drift further, but the point estimate of 89 represents only a modest appreciation, consistent with a low-volatility, slow-trend environment rather than any strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which is driven by the compounding of daily uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is quite tight because price movements within a single session tend to be constrained absent a major catalyst. At one week, the interval widens to reflect the possibility of several meaningful daily moves accumulating in either direction. By one month, the interval spans roughly 18 points, capturing the realistic range of outcomes when macro data releases, central bank communications, and shifting risk appetite can all materially reprice the asset over four weeks.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward greater hawkishness, or a broader risk-off episode driven by geopolitical developments could push prices well below 80 at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a strong positive surprise in economic fundamentals, a dovish pivot signal, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 98 or beyond. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves that would otherwise be contained.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility were to spike — for example, due to a credit event, a major geopolitical shock, or an unexpected earnings or data release — the true distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my confidence intervals imply. My stated 90% intervals should therefore be treated as reasonable central-case bounds under normal conditions rather than hard limits on what is possible.
